newsitem.title: USA: Defense begins case in du Pont trial.
newsitem.headline: Defense begins case in du Pont trial.

text.p: Lawyers for millionaire murder defendant John du Pont began their case Thursday, presenting witnesses to support a defence that du Pont was insane when he shot Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.

Prosecutors wrapped up their case earlier on the fourth day of the trial, although they are to return with a rebuttal expected to challenge psychiatric testimony likely to be the heart of du Pont's defence.

Du Pont attorney Thomas Bergstrom conceded on the first day of the trial on Monday that du Pont shot and killed Schultz Jan. 26, 1996. But Bergstrom said du Pont was afflicted with paraniod-schizophrenia and incapable of knowing what he was doing was wrong.
The first witness called by Bergstrom was Newtown Township Police Chief Lee Hunter, who described an interview with du Pont regarding a 1995 complaint that a wrestler on his estate attacked him.
Du Pont was an avid fan and patron of amateur wrestling, and maintained a training facility on his suburban Philadelphia estate where Schutlz and other wrestlers trained and lived.

Hunter, who was then a police lieutenant, said du Pont told him there was an international conspiracy to eject him from the wrestling world and threatened catastrophe if the conspiracy were not investigated.
"The entire Russian Army would engage in the ultimate war in Newtown Township," du Pont was quoted as saying in Hunter's police report.
"This is a conspiracy to kill the Holy Child," du Pont said, according to Hunter's report.

Schultz's widow, Nancy, testified Monday to the same incident, saying du Pont had come to their house drunk and in a rage over another wrestler who had moved off the estate, and hit his head in a fall.
Also testifying Thursday was Springfield Township police detective John Ryan, an early member of the team which negotiated with du Pont during a 48-hour standoff that followed Schultz's killing.
Ryan testified that du Pont in a telephone conversation with his bodyguard, who was assisting police, insisted that he was the American president and had "negotiated nuclear arms."
Ryan also said the bodyguard, relating the conversation with du Pont as it was proceeding, said du Pont told him, "We're in charge. You have federal authority. The local police must obey you."

In addition, du Pont's maintenance manager, Walter Fitzgerald, described several instances of eccentric behaviour by du Pont, such as an order by du Pont, after his arrest, to remove pilings on the estate to release "spirits."
Earlier in the day, the prosecution concluded its case by presenting a weapons expert and the doctor who performed the autopsy of the slain Schultz.
At the display of autopsy photographs, Nancy Schultz, who has been present for the course of the trial, left the room and several jurors were visibly moved.
